name: TYPE
description: TYPE returns a numeric code indicating the data type of a value: 1 for number, 2 for text, 4 for logical, 16 for error, and 64 for array.
tldr: Returns a number code for a value's type.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value, cell reference, or formula result whose type is tested.

basicExample.explanation: "x" is text, so the type code is 2.

advancedExamples.title: Detect an array
advancedExamples.scenario: A multi-cell range reference is an array.
advancedExamples.description: Reference a range to get code 64
advancedExamples.explanation: A range covering multiple cells is treated as an array, returning 64.

advancedExamples.title: Classify a logical value
advancedExamples.explanation: TRUE is a logical value, so the type code is 4.

howItWorks: TYPE examines the supplied value and returns an integer: 1 (number), 2 (text), 4 (logical TRUE/FALSE), 16 (error value), or 64 (array). It is useful inside branching logic when a formula must handle different input types differently.

howToSteps.name: Pick the value
howToSteps.text: Select the cell or value to classify.

limitations: Returns 64 for any array, even a single-cell array.
Cannot distinguish sub-types; dates and numbers both return 1.
Returns a code, not TRUE/FALSE, so compare it (e.g. =TYPE(x)=2).

commonErrors.cause: A multi-cell range reference is an array.
commonErrors.fix: Reference a single cell if you want codes 1, 2, or 4.

commonErrors.cause: TYPE returns a code, not TRUE/FALSE.
commonErrors.fix: Combine with a comparison, e.g. =TYPE(x)=2 for text.

googleSheetsEquivalent.description: TYPE works identically in Google Sheets with the same syntax and code values.

faq.question: What does 64 mean?
faq.answer: It means the value is an array.
